item.title: The hill I will die on: Cheques are still the best way to pay for things | Claire Jackson
item.author: Claire Jackson
item.content:encoded: A debit card might be quicker and easier, but there are thrills big and small to be had from whipping out your chequebookIt often takes other people to identify your quirks. Mine is writing cheques, a fact I was made aware of recently by a younger colleague, who watched with bemusement as I filled one out. He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. He looked on as I, a millennial, wrote “one hundred and forty-one pounds and thirty pence only”, that last word thrilling in its assertiveness – I will pay my bill, South East Water, and not a penny more!Having examined the whole procedure, including my procuring a stamp and envelope to send it off, he concluded – as so many have – that the process would be far better executed online. A friend also politely fed back that, although she appreciates how I “enclose a cheque” in every birthday card to her daughter, could I perhaps just do a bank transfer like everyone else?Claire Jackson is a journalist who writes about classical music, art and animalsContinue reading...

item.title: Grand Theft Anthropic: how GTA can inspire a fightback against AI | Alexander Hurst
item.author: Alexander Hurst
item.content:encoded: Tech billionaires are taking us for a ride. But new ‘poison pill’ software could help shield human-made creative output from hijacking Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI.On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there. Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from ParisContinue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
item.author: Editorial
item.content:encoded: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionairesFor the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.Continue reading...

item.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous

In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. item.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
item.author: Frédéric Noy
item.content:encoded: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technicalIn the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric NoyContinue reading...

item.title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
item.author: Dara Kerr
item.content:encoded: Elon Musk and Sam Altman among those rejoicing but Google, Meta and Apple chiefs have declined to weigh inThe phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.Continue reading...

item.title: Share your most outrageous experience when trying to rent a room in the UK
item.author: Guardian community team
item.content:encoded: We’d like to hear your stories of trying to find flatmates in the private rental market in the UK. Have you had to audition? What demands or restrictive rules have you encountered?Finding a room to rent in the UK has become intensely competitive, with prices rising and the number of rooms available shrinking. In big cities, prospective tenants often find they are competing with dozens of applicants for a single room - with potential housemates imposing increasingly specific and unusual demands.We would like to hear your experiences of trying to find flatmates in the private rental market. Have you sent dozens of applications without success? Have you had to go through lenghty interviews or flatmate “auditions” to secure a space? Have you encountered bizarre or restrictive rules, such as bans on working from home, or strict requirements around profession and lifestyle?Continue reading...
